justification: Measure-only by instruction: one read-only sweep script and two tracker entries. No product code, no served output, no database write. Not Minor, because the sweep's tiering is a judgement that will drive which tests get adjudicated first, and a wrong tier hides a served hazard field in tier 4 where nobody looks. The classifier deserves the same scrutiny as a gate.

falsifiable_check.fails_when: The sweep is falsifiable against a case with a known answer: the six flood tests that WERE pinning the defect are gone from the codebase (rewritten in #892), and the sweep correctly no longer reports them; the test that replaced them, tests/test_flood_normalise.py::test_epi_absent_is_unknown_not_a_clearance, asserts `is None` and is correctly NOT a candidate. Run against #892's parent commit it would have flagged them. It goes wrong in two directions and both are checkable by reading the output: a MISS if a test setting up an absence and asserting a negative does not appear (verified by hand against lot-search.test.ts:297, which does appear, in tier 1); a FALSE POSITIVE if a test asserting a genuine negative appears, which many do and is expected — test_overlay_absent_is_false_only_when_layer_covered and test_heritage_lists_are_three_state are both already correct and both appear. The tiering is checkable the same way: `--tier 1` must contain the flood, bushfire, heritage and contaminated-land hits and must not contain extraction-pipeline tests. The one confirmed defect was verified against the code, not the test: frontend-nextjs/app/api/lot-search/route.ts:195-197 literally reads `r.heritage ?? false`.
falsifiable_check.external_authority: The assertion text and the fixture shape come from test files this change does not write, and the confirmed defect was verified against route.ts, a file the sweep does not read. The sweep proposes; the code disposes.

pre_impl.existing_data: Four sweeps for prior art, recorded in the script header: scripts/check_test_baselines.py and check_dependency_skips.py count tests and skips and never read an assertion; no grep for absence-negative phrasing returns anything outside the flood tests that prompted this; scripts/mutation_health.py asks whether a test CAN fail, which is DQ-53's question and explicitly a different one; and DQ-53 itself is scoped to can't-fail tests. The corpus is 200 tracked Python test files and 81 TS/TSX ones.
pre_impl.assumption_mismatch: I expected tier 1 to be mostly defects and it is mostly correct code. A large share of the 55 tier-1 candidates are tests that already draw the distinction properly, and their NAMES say so — test_overlay_absent_is_false_only_when_layer_covered, test_heritage_lists_are_three_state, test_contaminated_failure_vs_genuinely_none_are_distinct, test_flood_ems_false_is_checked_clear_not_none. That is evidence the typed-absence work in #872/#873 landed in more places than the flood verdict, and it means the sweep's value is triage order rather than a defect list. Reporting a 55-item tier 1 as 55 defects would have been the wrong conclusion from the right data.
pre_impl.external_source_error: No external source is consulted. The only subprocess is `git ls-files`; if it fails the script prints UNKNOWABLE and exits 2 rather than reporting zero candidates, because an empty sweep and an unrun sweep must not look alike. A test file that will not parse is skipped silently by ast — stated here as a known under-report rather than surfaced per-file, since a syntactically broken test file already fails collection and is visible elsewhere.
pre_impl.frontend_type: The TS half has no stdlib parser, so it is line-based over the window from the enclosing it()/test() to the assertion. That is weaker than the Python ast pass and will miss an absence set up outside the block or in a shared fixture, and can attribute a neighbouring line to the wrong test when blocks nest. Stated in the module docstring. It found the one confirmed defect regardless.
pre_impl.user_failure_mode: Nobody reads a 233-line list, adjudicates none of it, and the sweep becomes a file that exists rather than a thing that changed an outcome — the failure mode of every audit. Mitigated only by the tiering and by naming ONE confirmed defect at the top with its file and line, so there is a first move rather than a backlog.
pre_impl.new_vs_existing: New script, no new gate, nothing wired into a hook. It reuses the tracker as the place findings live, because a finding that exists only in a chat message is the doc-decay failure this campaign exists to stop.

functions.name: sweep_python
functions.input: the tracked Python test files, parsed with ast rather than matched by line
functions.output: candidates where one test function both sets up an absence and asserts a negative verdict
functions.if_none: a file that will not parse is skipped, which under-reports; an empty result means no pairing was found, never that the sweep did not run

functions.name: sweep_typescript
functions.input: the tracked TS/TSX test files, scanned line-wise within the enclosing it() or test() block
functions.output: candidates where a null, empty or throwing case sits in the same block as a toBe(false)
functions.if_none: weaker than the Python pass by construction and will miss an absence set up in a shared fixture; the limit is stated rather than implied

functions.name: _tier_for
functions.input: the test file path and the assertion text, matched against keyword groups per tier
functions.output: how much a wrong False would cost the reader, worst first, as a triage order not a severity claim
functions.if_none: anything unmatched falls to tier 4, so a served field with an unfamiliar name lands where nobody looks — the sweep's own worst failure mode

values.value: 233 candidates: 55 tier-1, 33 tier-2, 65 tier-3, 80 tier-4, across 200 Python and 81 TS/TSX test files
values.if_missing: git ls-files failing prints UNKNOWABLE and exits 2 rather than reporting zero

values.value: 80.1% of 151 stored flood reports carry no council name from the SES lookup — 109 of 109 rows that were queried and fell outside every study extent, plus 12 never queried
values.read_at: production property_reports, one read-only SELECT over product='flood', 2026-08-08
values.if_missing: no DATABASE_URL means the rate is unknown, and the policy question stays open rather than being decided on a guess

queries.purpose: count how often the SES lookup returns no council name, split by whether it matched, missed or never ran
queries.file_line: ad-hoc read-only SELECT, recorded in DQ-57 rather than committed as a script
queries.where_clause: WHERE product = 'flood' — SELECT only, statement_timeout 30s, no UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE

break_it.scenario: A served hazard field has a name none of the tier keyword groups match, so its test lands in tier 4 among the extraction plumbing.
break_it.what_happens: It is ranked where nobody looks, and the sweep's whole purpose — order the adjudication by what a wrong answer costs — silently fails for that field. This is the sweep's own worst failure mode and it is the same shape as the defect it hunts.
break_it.how: Not mitigated. The keyword groups are explicit and listed at the top of the script so they can be read and extended, but nothing verifies they cover every served field. Adjudicating tier 1 should start by checking the group list against the served contract, not by trusting it.

break_it.scenario: Someone reads the 55 tier-1 candidates as 55 defects and opens 55 issues.
break_it.what_happens: Most are correct code. A False is the right answer when a source was consulted and said no; only an unreached source makes it wrong, and the two are indistinguishable from test text.
break_it.how: The script prints that sentence above the results, the tracker entry repeats it, and three already-correct examples are named so the reader sees the shape of a non-defect before scrolling.

break_it.scenario: The TS pass attributes an assertion to the wrong test because it() blocks nest or a helper sits between them.
break_it.what_happens: A candidate is reported against a test that did not make the assertion, wasting a reviewer's time, or an absence set up in beforeEach is missed entirely and a real candidate never appears.
break_it.how: Not mitigated — TypeScript has no stdlib parser and adding one is disproportionate for a triage tool. The limit is in the module docstring and in this report. The Python half, which covers 200 of the 281 files, is ast-based and does not have this weakness.

break_it.scenario: The SES rate is read as a reason to flip the default and mark an unknown council as not-assessed.
break_it.what_happens: 80% of flood reports would render 'not assessed', which destroys the signal the three-state change exists to create — the same failure inverted, exactly as with the statewide study-absence scoping in #892.
break_it.how: DQ-57 states the rate first and the implication second: the number rules out both defaults and points at lookup_lga, which resolves LGA statewide from spatial_overlays and already has a connection available in this module.

break_it.scenario: The SES count is re-run later, returns a different rate, and the policy conclusion in DQ-57 is quietly left standing on the old number.
break_it.what_happens: The conclusion — that neither default works and lookup_lga is the right signal — depends on the rate being high. If a future SES coverage improvement drops it to a few percent, treating an unknown council as not-assessed becomes viable and the recorded recommendation would be wrong.
break_it.how: DQ-57 records the query, the split (30 matched / 109 queried-and-outside / 12 never queried) and the date, not just the headline percentage, so a re-run can be compared against the same three buckets rather than one number. The 100% figure for the queried-and-outside bucket is the load-bearing one and it is structural: ses_study_lga is populated only by a study match.
break_it.repro: SELECT outputs->>'ses_in_flood_planning_area', outputs->>'ses_study_lga' FROM property_reports WHERE product='flood'

mutation_analysis: Classical mutation testing does not apply to a read-only triage script, so the equivalent was done against a case with a known answer. The six flood tests that genuinely pinned the defect were rewritten in #892; the sweep correctly does not report their replacements, which assert `is None`. Removing the absence requirement makes every negative assertion a candidate and the count explodes past 1,000 — visible immediately. Removing the negative requirement reports every absence test regardless of what it asserts. Collapsing the tiers to one destroys the only thing that makes 233 items actionable. The one confirmed defect was checked against route.ts rather than accepted from the test, which is the check that matters: the sweep's output is a hypothesis and the source file is the authority.
residual_risk: 233 candidates are unadjudicated and this change adjudicates one. That is the honest state: the sweep converts an unknown into a ranked list, and a ranked list nobody works through is worth very little more than the unknown was. The tiering is keyword-based and its failure mode — a served field falling to tier 4 — is unmitigated and is the same shape as the defect being hunted. The TS half is line-based and will both miss and misattribute. The SES rate is measured on 151 rows from one product on one deployment; it is decisive for flood and should not be generalised to how often lookup_lga would succeed, which was not measured. Nothing here changes behaviour, so the risk of this PR is entirely the risk of a false sense that the class has been dealt with.

post_merge.db_reset: No. One read-only SELECT was run during measurement; nothing was written.
post_merge.secrets: No credentials are read by the sweep; the SES measurement used the existing .env and logged none.
post_merge.manual_verify: Yes. Adjudicate tier 1, starting with lot-search.route.ts:195-197, and before trusting the ranking check the tier keyword groups at the top of the script against the served field contract — a served field whose name matches nothing lands in tier 4.
